name: Tea (green or black tea, Camellia sinensis, as a drink)
short: Very hot tea linked to oesophageal cancer (observational). Case reports: hepatitis after green or black tea; bone fluorosis; severe iron-deficiency anaemia. Green tea cut nadolol levels 85%.
text: This entry covers tea brewed from Camellia sinensis (green, black and similar teas) as a drink; concentrated green tea extracts have their own entry, and herbal teas from other plants are not covered. Cancer (observational evidence): a 2022 meta-analysis of 23 observational reports (5,050 cases and 10,609 controls) found a higher risk of oesophageal cancer with drinking tea at higher temperature (odds ratio 1.79), significant for squamous cell carcinoma but not adenocarcinoma, and a 2019 umbrella review of meta-analyses found harmful associations with oesophageal and gastric cancer when tea was drunk at more than 55 to 60 °C, while concluding that tea, except very hot tea, seems generally safe at usual intakes; these are associations, not proof of cause. Liver (case reports): a teenager who had drunk 1.5 to 2 litres of black iced tea a day for three months developed hepatitis with gallbladder sludge after other causes were excluded, and recovered within two months of stopping; a previously healthy 16-year-old girl had acute hepatitis after 3 months of regular Chinese green tea bought online, with rapid recovery after stopping; and a further case report describes severe hepatitis related to drinking green tea in a 2-year-old child. Bones (case reports): skeletal fluorosis, with severe bone and joint pain and abnormally dense bones, developed in a 48-year-old woman who drank 1 to 2 gallons of brewed tea daily for more than three decades, and in a 49-year-old woman who drank 2 gallons of extra-strength instant tea daily since age 12. Kidneys: a 2015 letter with no abstract is titled as describing a case of iced-tea nephropathy. Iron: a review describes tea as a dietary factor that inhibits iron absorption, which it says may matter for people with low intakes of iron from meat and of absorption enhancers such as vitamin C; from its calculation model, it also concludes that enough of these enhancers in the diet (vitamin C, meat, fish or poultry) overcomes the inhibition even from large amounts of tea. A 2024 case report describes severe iron-deficiency anaemia in a woman after short-term, moderate green tea drinking; the authors note that a fall in haemoglobin of 6.9 g/dl solely from moderate tea drinking over three months is uncommon, and the anaemia did not recur after she changed her tea intake. Interactions: in 10 healthy volunteers, 14 days of green tea lowered the peak level and total exposure of a single dose of the blood-pressure medicine nadolol by about 85% and reduced its effect on systolic blood pressure. In a crossover study in 16 healthy adults, taking the medicine raloxifene with a well-characterised green tea, on 1 day or on the fifth day after 4 days of daily green tea, lowered total raloxifene exposure to about 60% of that with water, below the range the investigators had set in advance as no effect; the abstract does not say how the tea was prepared. A case report describes a woman with a liver transplant whose tacrolimus levels rose above the target range, with abdominal pain and nausea, after heavy drinking of non-commercial green tea with orange extract; levels returned to normal within 24 hours of pausing tacrolimus and stopping the tea. A 2021 systematic review lists green tea among foods and herbs associated with increased bleeding risk in people taking warfarin; it reports that 20 herbs and supplements were linked to bleeding, including intracranial bleeding that led to death, but the abstract does not say which products those major events involved. On the other side, in 11 healthy volunteers brewed green tea did not change blood levels of fluvastatin.
